_schema: Government Hack image manifest for the Unit 1 Teacher Deck. Per standard: an 'anchor' primary-source VISUAL (document scan, period political cartoon, or portrait). Mirrors HistoryHack_Platinum/build/unit1_images.json. file = expected asset path under assets/primary_sources/; if the binary is not yet present the deck renders a cited source frame in its place.
_rule: Curated genuine public-domain works only. Citations are accurate at the work + repository level. Nothing fabricated. Actual image files must be procured from the cited repository (public domain) and dropped at the given file path; naming convention GC.NN_slug.jpg mirrors the US History Hack bank.
_rights_note: All works listed are in the public domain in the United States: U.S. government documents, or works published before 1929, or works whose creators died more than 95 years ago. Verify the specific digital reproduction's terms at the repository before publishing.

anchor.title: Portrait of John Locke
anchor.creator: Sir Godfrey Kneller
anchor.caption: John Locke (1632–1704), whose Second Treatise of Government argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed — a direct root of American political thought.
anchor.alt_en: Painted portrait of John Locke, an English philosopher in dark robes, seated and facing slightly right.
anchor.alt_es: Retrato pintado de John Locke, filósofo inglés con toga oscura, sentado y mirando ligeramente a la derecha.

anchor.title: Declaration of Independence (engrossed copy)
anchor.creator: Second Continental Congress; engrossed by Timothy Matlack
anchor.caption: The engrossed Declaration of Independence, 1776 — the document that turned the colonists' grievances into a claim of natural rights and self-government.
anchor.alt_en: Aged parchment of the Declaration of Independence with the bold heading and columns of signatures below the text.
anchor.alt_es: Pergamino envejecido de la Declaración de Independencia con el encabezado en negrita y columnas de firmas debajo del texto.

anchor.title: Join, or Die
anchor.creator: Benjamin Franklin
anchor.repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
anchor.caption: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' (1754): a severed snake labeled with the colonies. Under the loose Articles of Confederation, the states struggled to act as one — the cartoon's warning about disunity still fit.
anchor.alt_en: Woodcut of a snake cut into segments, each labeled with the initials of a colony, above the words JOIN, or DIE.
anchor.alt_es: Grabado de una serpiente cortada en segmentos, cada uno con las iniciales de una colonia, sobre las palabras JOIN, or DIE.

anchor.title: The Looking Glass for 1787
anchor.creator: Amos Doolittle
anchor.repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
anchor.caption: A 1787 cartoon of Connecticut's ratification debate — a wagon of state pulled in opposite directions. It captures the Federalist vs. Anti-Federalist struggle over the new Constitution.
anchor.alt_en: Engraved cartoon showing figures pulling a loaded wagon in opposite directions, with speech captions, representing a political dispute.
anchor.alt_es: Caricatura grabada que muestra figuras tirando de un carro cargado en direcciones opuestas, con leyendas, que representa una disputa política.

anchor.title: U.S. Constitution, Page 1 (“We the People”)
anchor.creator: Constitutional Convention; engrossed by Jacob Shallus
anchor.caption: The first page of the Constitution opens with the Preamble — 'We the People' — stating the purposes government exists to serve.
anchor.alt_en: First parchment page of the U.S. Constitution with the large opening words 'We the People' in ornate script.
anchor.alt_es: Primera página en pergamino de la Constitución de EE. UU. con las grandes palabras iniciales 'We the People' en letra adornada.

anchor.title: The Federalist, Volume 1 (title page)
anchor.creator: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay ('Publius')
anchor.repository: Library of Congress, Rare Book & Special Collections
anchor.caption: The Federalist (1788). In No. 51, Madison argued that a government of separated, checking powers is necessary 'because men are not angels' — the logic of limited government.
anchor.alt_en: Printed 1788 title page reading 'THE FEDERALIST: A Collection of Essays' with publisher details below.
anchor.alt_es: Página de título impresa de 1788 que dice 'THE FEDERALIST: A Collection of Essays' con datos del editor debajo.

anchor.title: The Federal Edifice (“The Federal Pillars”)
anchor.creator: Massachusetts Centinel
anchor.repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
anchor.caption: The 'Federal Pillars' cartoon (1788) shows states rising as columns of the new structure — a fitting image for the Constitution's architecture and its deliberately hard amendment process.
anchor.alt_en: Cartoon of classical columns, each labeled with a state, being raised to form the roof of a building labeled for the federal government.
anchor.alt_es: Caricatura de columnas clásicas, cada una con el nombre de un estado, que se levantan para formar el techo de un edificio del gobierno federal.

anchor.title: The Bill of Rights (engrossed copy)
anchor.creator: 1st U.S. Congress
anchor.caption: The engrossed Bill of Rights, 1789. The first eight Amendments each draw a boundary government may not cross; the 9th and 10th reserve rights and powers to the people and the states.
anchor.alt_en: Parchment page listing the proposed Articles of amendment that became the Bill of Rights, in columns of handwritten text.
anchor.alt_es: Página de pergamino que enumera los artículos de enmienda propuestos que se convirtieron en la Declaración de Derechos, en columnas de texto manuscrito.

anchor.title: Great Seal of the United States (obverse)
anchor.creator: Charles Thomson & William Barton (design)
anchor.repository: U.S. National Archives / public domain (U.S. government emblem)
anchor.caption: The Great Seal's motto, E Pluribus Unum — 'out of many, one' — captures the constitutional republic: many states and citizens under one representative government limited by law.
anchor.alt_en: The obverse of the Great Seal of the United States: an eagle holding an olive branch and arrows, with a shield and a banner reading E Pluribus Unum.
anchor.alt_es: El anverso del Gran Sello de los Estados Unidos: un águila que sostiene una rama de olivo y flechas, con un escudo y una cinta que dice E Pluribus Unum.
